slides.title: Which card protects you?
slides.sub: Debit vs. credit: federal law caps your fraud losses differently on each.

slides.heading: Credit cards: $50 max
body: By law, the most you'll owe for unauthorized charges on a credit card is $50. If thieves got only your card number, not the card, you generally owe nothing.
Report a lost card before it's used and you can't be held responsible for any charges.

slides.heading: Debit cards: it depends
body: Report within 2 business days of learning your card is lost or stolen and you owe at most $50. Miss that, but report within 60 days of your statement: up to $500.
Wait longer and you could be on the hook for everything taken after that.
slides.source: Regulation E, via Federal Reserve, Oct. 2025

slides.heading: The real difference
body: Debit fraud pulls your own money out of your account while it gets sorted out. Credit card fraud uses the bank's money.
Many card networks also promise $0 liability on debit fraud, but that's a network policy on top of the law.

slides.takeaway: Shopping online? Use a credit card you pay in full, and check your accounts often.

posts.caption:
Shopping online for Black Friday? The card you pay with changes how much fraud can cost you.

Credit cards: by law, the most you'll owe for unauthorized charges is $50, and if only your card number was stolen (not the card), you generally owe nothing (CFPB).

Debit cards: it depends on how fast you report. Within 2 business days of learning your card was lost or stolen, you're liable for at most $50. Within 60 days of your statement, up to $500. After that, you could be liable for everything taken. Many card networks add their own $0-liability policies, but debit fraud still takes your own cash out of your account while it's sorted out.

Data: CFPB; Federal Reserve Consumer Compliance Outlook (Oct. 2025) on Regulation E.
